Software Security Project Requirements 
1. Application: 
Each team must be composed of 6 members (3 Red Team and 3 Blue Team) . The team must design and build a small 
e-commerce website, “SecureShop”, and make it resistant to the vulnerabilities and attacks covered in this course. 
Both the features and the security of the website are graded. 
Each feature is a possible entry point for an attacker, so everyone is part of the website’s attack surface: every point 
where an attacker can send input or trigger an action, such as forms, URLs, request parameters and admin pages. 
2. Functional Requirements: 
The website must include the following features (points are out of 100, see item 8): 
o Registration and login: create an account, confirm it, log in and log out (5) 
o Product catalogue: product list and detail pages, with search or filtering (4) 
o Shopping cart: add, remove and change quantity; the cart is kept during the session (4) 
o Coupons and newsletter: apply coupon codes at checkout; newsletter signup issues a coupon (3) 
o Checkout and orders: pay with store credit, show an order confirmation, keep order history (5) 
o User account page: view and update profile details, and view own orders (3) 
o Admin panel: manage users, products and coupons (4) 
o Usability: clear navigation, helpful error messages, works on desktop and mobile (2) 
A missing or broken feature cannot be made up for by strong security. Extra features beyond this list can earn bonus 
points if they work well and are secured. 
3. Security Requirements: 
The website must be protected against every vulnerability and attack taught in the course. 
 
For each topic, students must show that the attack works against a naive implementation and fails against their own. 
o Apply each topic to every feature where it is relevant, not just one. 
o Build the defenses into the application itself. Do not rely on the environment or on hidden pages for protection. 
o Test with unexpected input and unexpected sequences of actions, not only the normal path. 
o Keep a Security Coverage Matrix  throughout the project, with one row per topic: the attack scenario in 
SecureShop, the root cause, the defense implemented, where it is in the code, and the evidence.

4. Security Testing: 
Students must test their own website the way an attacker would: 
o Step 1, self -test: using the testing tools from the labs, try to break the website for every row of the Security 
Coverage Matrix. Fix what breaks and keep the evidence. 
o Step 2, Red Team vs Blue Team: the 3 Red Team members attack the website built by the Blue Team within a 
fixed time window and report each finding: what was tried, the request used, the result, and the severity. The 
Blue Team members then fix valid findings and document them. 
5. Project Documentation: 
Students must submit: 
o Source code in a Git repository, with a meaningful commit history from every team member 
o README with setup steps, test accounts (a normal user and an admin), and a one-page architecture overview 
o Security Design Report (about 8-12 pages): threat model (assets, entry points, attackers) and the complete 
Security Coverage Matrix 
o Attack Evidence Report: evidence that each attack taught in the course fails against the team’s website 
o Red Team Penetration Test Report on the team’s own website 
6. Demonstration: 
Students must demonstrate a working website in a live demo (10 -15 minutes) followed by Q&A. Each team member 
must answer questions about their own part. 
7. Grading: 
The project is scored out of 100 and converted to 20 marks. Each phase is scored with the areas that apply to it, and the 
result is converted to that phase’s marks (5 for Phase 1, awarded at the Week 10 discussion, and 15 for Phase 2).

o Attack only your own team’s website, inside the course environment and within the agreed time window. 
o Never test real websites, other students’ machines, or university systems without written permission. Do not use

What is PortSwigger?

What is PortSwigger?
● PortSwigger is the industry-standard web application security testing toolkit.
● It also runs the Web Security Academy: a free, hands-on training platform used by 
students, bug bounty hunters, and professional penetration testers worldwide.
● The Academy pairs clear written theory with real, deliberately vulnerable lab 
environments — so you learn by actually exploiting the bug, not just reading about 
it.
● This course's labs are taken directly from the Academy.
HTTP Basics

HTTP Basics
HTTP Headers
● A request has 3 parts: Method, Path, Host
● GET = retrieve a page
● POST = send data (like a login form)
● Example: GET /login HTTP/1.1
GET /login HTTP/1.1

Why is this needed? 
Websites use HTTPS, which encrypts traffic.
Without Burp's certificate, your browser will block

certificate tells your browser: "Trust Burp Suite it's
allowed to intercept."

What is a Proxy?
• A proxy sits between your browser and the 
internet.
• It intercepts requests before they leave your 
computer.
• Burp catches requests so you can read, edit, 
and replay them

What is the Site 
Map? 
• As you browse a website through Burp's 
proxy, Burp automatically records every page 
and request you visited. 
• This is called the Site Map - it builds a visual 
tree of the website's structure.
• Useful for recon - finding hidden pages and 
API endpoints

What is 
Repeater? 
• Repeater lets you take a single HTTP request 
and send it over and over, modifying it each 
time. Instead of re-doing an action in the 
browser, you can tweak the request directly 
and instantly see the server's response
How it works:
● Go to Proxy → HTTP history
● Find a request you want to experiment with
● Right-click → Send to Repeater (Or CTRL + R)
● Go to the Repeater tab
● You'll see the raw request on the left
● Modify anything you want (a parameter, a header, 
etc.)
● Click Send
● The response appears on the right

What is 
Intruder? 
• Intruder is Burp's automated attack tool. You 
take a request, mark one or more values as 
payload positions (spots to inject), give it a list 
of values, and Intruder will automatically send 
the request for every value in your list.
How it works:
● Capture a request in Proxy → HTTP history
● Right-click → Send to Intruder (OR CTRL + i)
● Go to Intruder → Positions
● Burp auto-highlights guessed positions - click Clear § to remove 
them
● Highlight the value you want to fuzz, click Add §
● Go to Payloads tab
● Add your payload list (type manually or load a file)
● Click Start Attack
● Watch the results - look for different Status Codes or 
Response Lengths

Business Logic Vulnerabilities
● Flaws in an app's design/implementation that let an attacker trigger unintended 
behavior by misusing legitimate functionality.
● They arise from flawed assumptions about how users (and attackers) will 
interact with the system — not from a broken line of code.

Lab 1: Excessive Trust in Client-Side 
Controls

Business Logic Vulnerabilities
Objective: buy the “Lightweight l33t leather jacket” even though its price is far above your available store credit.
Credentials: log in with wiener : peter
The bug: the shop sends the item's price to the server as a normal, editable request parameter — and the server trusts it

Confirm the Price 
Change in the Cart

Never trust data that only the client can see or control — recompute prices, quantities, and totals from the server's 
own source of truth on every request.

Lab 2.1: Flawed Enforcement of Business 
Rules

Lab 2.1: Objective
● Objective: exploit the coupon logic in the purchasing workflow to buy the “Lightweight l33t leather jacket”.
● Credentials: wiener : peter
● The bug: the app only rejects a coupon if it is the same as the last one applied, so alternating between two codes applies 
them repeatedly.
● Lab link: portswigger.net/web-security/logic-flaws/examples/lab-logic-flaws-flawed-enforcement-of-business-rules
1. Collect 2 coupons
 2. Add jacket, checkout
 3. Alternate the codes
 4. Place order

Collect the 
Coupon Codes
STEP 1 / 4
● Log in and notice the coupon code NEWCUST5 shown on 
the site.
● At the bottom of the page, sign up to the newsletter.
● You receive a second coupon code: SIGNUP30.

Apply Both 
Coupons
STEP 2 / 4
● Add the leather jacket to your cart.
● Go to the checkout and apply both coupon codes.
● The order total drops by a discount for each code.

Bypass the 
Coupon Check
STEP 3 / 4
● Apply the same code twice in a row: it is rejected as 
already applied.
● Now alternate between the two codes: NEWCUST5, 
SIGNUP30, NEWCUST5, SIGNUP30 …
● Each one is accepted, so the discount keeps stacking.

Reduce the 
Total & Order
STEP 4 / 4
● Keep alternating the codes until the total is below your 
store credit.
● Click Place order.
● The lab shows “Congratulations, you solved the lab!”

Lab 2.1: Root Cause & How to Prevent It
Root cause
● The rule “each coupon can be used once” is enforced 
badly: only the most recent code is remembered.
● The developer assumed users would apply codes in a 
simple sequence, not alternate them.
● No cap exists on the total discount.
How to prevent it
● Store all applied coupons on the order and reject any code 
already in that set.
● Enforce limits server-side: one use per code, and a cap on 
the maximum discount.
● Re-validate the full cart, discounts and total at checkout.
● Test business rules with unexpected sequences, not only 
the happy path.

Lab 2.2: Root Cause & How to Prevent It
Root cause
● The app handles the same input differently in different 
places: the full address is used to send the email, but only 
255 characters are stored.
● The developer assumed users would never enter an email 
that long.
● Admin access is granted from the email domain, so the 
truncated value passes the check.
How to prevent it
● Enforce one maximum length at the start and reject over-
long input instead of silently truncating it.
● Validate the exact value that will be stored and used.
● Do not grant privileges from an email domain; assign roles 
explicitly.
● Test exceptional input: very long, empty, and special 
values.
Lab 2.3: Insufficient Workflow Validation

Lab 2.3: Objective
● Objective: buy the “Lightweight l33t leather jacket” by abusing the purchasing workflow.
● Credentials: wiener : peter
● The bug: the app assumes users reach the order confirmation page only after a successful checkout and does not verify that 
the order was paid for.
● Lab link: portswigger.net/web-security/logic-flaws/examples/lab-logic-flaws-insufficient-workflow-validation
1. Buy an affordable item
 2. Capture order-confirmation 
request
 3. Add jacket to cart
 4. Replay confirmation

Buy a Cheap 
Item
STEP 1 / 4
● With Burp running, log in as wiener : peter.
● Buy any item that you can afford with your store credit.

Study the Order 
Flow
STEP 2 / 4
● Open Proxy → HTTP history.
● When you place an order, POST /cart/checkout redirects 
you to an order confirmation page.
● Send GET /cart/order-confirmation?order-
confirmation=true to Burp Repeater.

Add the Jacket 
to Your Cart
STEP 3 / 4
● In the browser, add the “Lightweight l33t leather jacket” to 
your basket.
● Do not go through checkout: its price is far above your 
store credit.

Replay the 
Confirmation
STEP 4 / 4

● The order completes without the cost being deducted from 
your store credit.

Lab 2.3: Root Cause & How to Prevent It
Root cause
● The app does not validate the workflow: the confirmation 
step can be requested without completing checkout.
● It assumes users always follow the intended sequence of 
steps.
● Confirming the order never checks that payment was 
successful.
How to prevent it
● Track order state on the server and allow confirmation 
only after payment succeeds.
● Verify the cart total and payment at the final step, not just 
at checkout.
● Bind confirmation to a unique, unguessable order ID tied 
to the user session.
● Test by skipping, repeating and reordering steps of every 
workflow.
Thank you

How to look, before you change anything
1 Read the goal. Write whose account the lab asks you to reach, and which account is yours.
2 Walk the happy path. Log in, or request a reset, as yourself. List every step the application

3 Mark the trust boundary. In HTTP history, circle any field that names a user, a code, or a host. The

Lab 3.1   2FA broken logic

Lab 3.1  ·  2FA Broken Logic — Overview
1 The goal. Reach Carlos's account page without ever knowing his password.
2 Your credentials. wiener : peter — plus an email client to read your own 2FA code.
3 The feature. After a correct password, the app asks for a 4-digit code sent by email before it opens 
the account page.
4 The hint. Carlos never logs in himself during this lab — so every code must come from tricking the 
server, not from watching him.

Lab 3.1  ·  The Vulnerability, Step by Step
Log in as wiener
POST /login with valid credentials
Server sets a cookie
Set-Cookie: verify=wiener
Attacker edits the cookie
verify=wiener becomes verify=carlos
Server generates a 2FA code
The code is now valid for carlos
Brute-force the 4-digit code
POST /login2, mfa-code 0000–9999
302 redirect
Logged in as carlos

Lab 3.1  ·  Steps 1–4: Hijack the Session
1 1. Log in and observe. Sign in with wiener:peter and walk through 2FA. In POST /login2, the verify 
parameter says whose account is being checked.
2 2. Log out. Clear the session so the next request starts the verification flow fresh.
3 3. Hijack the cookie. In Burp Repeater, send GET /login2 and change verify=wiener to 
verify=carlos. The server now generates a 2FA code for Carlos.
4 4. Re-open verification. Log in again as yourself, then deliberately submit a wrong 2FA code — this 
cleanly re-opens the second step.

Lab 3.1  ·  Steps 5–8: Brute-Force and Win
1 5. Set up Intruder. Send the POST /login2 request to Burp Intruder.
2 6. Configure the attack. Keep verify=carlos fixed; mark mfa-code as the payload position. Brute-
force all 4-digit values, 0000–9999.
3 7. Spot the win. Every wrong guess returns the same 200 OK page. The correct code returns a 302 
redirect — that's the signal.
4 8. Finish. Load that 302 response in the browser and click My account — you're now logged in as 
Carlos.

Lab 3.1  ·  The 4 Key HTTP Requests
1 1. POST /login. Submits wiener's real credentials. Look at the response, not the request — the 
header Set-Cookie: verify=wiener is where the server first hands identity to the client.
2 2. GET /login2 (normal). Loads the 2FA entry page. This request automatically carries Cookie: 
verify=wiener — nothing else in it proves who's asking.
3
3. GET /login2 (hijacked, in Repeater). The same request, but with the cookie edited to 
verify=carlos. Response: still 200 OK — the server silently generates a fresh code for Carlos, no 
extra check.
4
4. POST /login2 with mfa-code (brute-force). Repeated for every 4-digit value. Wrong guesses 
return 200 with the same page; the correct one returns 302 Found with Location: /my-account — 
that's the signal.

Lab 3.1  ·  The verify Cookie — Root Cause
1 What it is. Name: verify. Value: a plain username. The server sets it the moment a password check 
succeeds — before any 2FA code exists.
2 Where it's set. In the Set-Cookie header of the POST /login response. The server never revisits or 
re-signs this value after that point.
3 Where it's read. Every request to /login2. The server trusts whatever username sits in this cookie 
to decide whose 2FA code to generate and check.
4
Why it's the bug. The value is 100% client-controlled — anyone can open DevTools or Burp and 
rewrite it. A secure design tracks identity server-side in the session; this one hands it to the 
browser and trusts it back unchanged.

What is Behavioral Authentication?
1 The old question.  Classic authentication asks “who are you?” once — a password or an OTP at the door. After that, it trusts you for the whole 
session.
2 The new question.  Behavioral authentication keeps asking “does this still act like you?” using patterns: typing rhythm, login time, location, 
and device.
3 Anomaly detection.  We learn each user’s normal behavior, then flag any login that is statistically far from that normal — a likely account 
takeover.
4 The response.  An anomaly does not always block. It often triggers step-up MFA — exactly the “never trust, always verify” idea of Zero Trust.

How to Think, Before You Code
1 1. Collect history.  Gather the user’s past, trusted logins. Each login becomes a row of numeric features (hour, typing speed, distance from 
home).
2 2. Learn “normal”.  For every feature compute the mean (the center) and the standard deviation (how much it usually varies).
3 3. Score the new login.  Measure how many standard deviations the new value is from the mean — this single number is the z-score.
4 4. Decide.  Average the z-scores. If the average is above a threshold, the behavior is abnormal → challenge or block it.

Lab 4.1  ·  The One Idea You Need — the z-score
The z-score answers: “how surprising is this value, compared to what’s normal?”

def totp(secret, when, step=30, digits=6):
    counter = int(when.timestamp()) // step
    digest = hmac.new(secret, pack('>Q', counter), sha1).digest()
    offset = digest[-1] & 0x0F
    binary = unpack('>I', digest[offset:offset + 4])[0] & 0x7FFFFFFF
    return the last 6 digits of binary

Security Terminologies in software
● Defects are implementation vulnerabilities and design vulnerabilities. 
● Bugs are implementation-level errors that can be detected and removed.
○ Example: Buffer overflow. 
● Flaws are problems at a deeper level. They are instantiated in the code and 
present or absent at design-level.
○ Example: Error-handling problems. 
● Failures are the inability of the software to perform its required function.
● Risks capture the probability that a flaw or a bug will impact the purpose of the 
software. 
○ Risk = probability x impact 
● Vulnerabilities are errors that an attacker can exploit. 
○ Either flaws in the design or flaws in the implementation.
○ Design-level vulnerabilities are the hardest defects to handle.

INTRODUCTION
What is Authentication? Security First Gateway
•  Authentication (AuthN): verifying that an entity (user, device, or service) is who or what it 
claims to be.
•  Authorization (AuthZ): deciding what an already-authenticated entity may do - always 
comes after AuthN.
•  Non-repudiation: authenticated actions are logged so the actor cannot later deny them.
•  A breach of the authentication layer defeats every control above it (RBAC, ABAC, 
encryption-at-rest...).
AuthN = identity proof  →  AuthZ = permission decision  →  Audit = accountability.

Knowledge-Based Authentication: Passwords
■  How It Works
• User registers a secret string; server stores a salted, slow one-way hash (never the plaintext).
• On login, the server hashes the submitted password with the stored salt and compares digests
•  Modern recommended hashing: Argon2id or bcrypt/scrypt – never fast hashes like MD5/SHA-1
■  Implementation Considerations
• Enforce breach-password screening (check against known-compromised lists, e.g., HaveIBeenPwned API)
• Use Argon2id/bcrypt with per-user salt + server-side pepper; rate-limit and lock out after failed attempts
• DISCOURAGES forced periodic rotation and arbitrary complexity rules

Knowledge-Based: Passwords
WHY does it exist?
Cheapest possible factor: no hardware, no enrollment logistics - every user already understands it.
HOW does it work?
• Registration: server stores a salted, slow one-way hash (argon2id) - never the plaintext.
• Login: server hashes the candidate and compares digests in constant time.
+  STRENGTHS
• Zero cost, works on every device.
• Only factor that works fully offline in the user's head - no device needed.

• Fast hashes (MD5/SHA-1) fall to GPUs at billions of guesses/second.
• Users pick weak secrets; helpdesk resets are a social-engineering target.
WHEN should you use it?
Always present as a fallback - but never alone for anything valuable; pair with MFA or migrate to passkeys.

PINs & Security Questions
WHY does it exist?
• A short secret optimized for speed on a single device - typing a 20-char password 50×/day is unusable.
HOW does it work?
• PIN never leaves the device: it unlocks a private key inside the TPM / secure enclave.
• Hardware lockout (anti-hammering): N wrong tries → exponential delay or wipe.
+  STRENGTHS
• Nothing secret transmitted to any server - server-side breach leaks no PINs.
• Short secret is safe BECAUSE verification is local and rate-limited in hardware.
−  WEAKNESSES
Shoulder surfing, smudge attacks, weak choices (1234, birth year).
Tied to one device - lose the device, re-enroll everywhere.
Security questions: public, low-entropy answers - NIST 800-63-4 bans them for recovery.
WHEN should you use it?
Local device unlock and passkey user-verification (Windows Hello PIN, phone lock screen).

In Step 1, the Server or Relying Party generates a

challenge.

Inherence-Based: Physiological Biometrics
WHY does it exist?
Nothing to remember, nothing to carry - the strongest usability of any factor.
HOW does it work?
• Sensor captures a trait (fingerprint ridges, face depth map, iris) → mathematical template.
• Matching is a similarity SCORE vs a threshold - probabilistic, not exact like a password.
• Modern model (FIDO/passkeys): template stays in the device secure enclave; it only unlocks a local key.
+  STRENGTHS
• Frictionless user verification; local-only biometric is phishing-resistant (never transmitted).
• Face ID-class sensors: claimed false-accept rate ~1 in 1,000,000 with liveness/depth.
−  WEAKNESSES
• IRREVOCABLE - you can't change your fingerprint after a template breach.
• Presentation attacks: lifted prints, photos, masks - needs liveness detection.
• FAR/FRR trade-off: stricter threshold locks out real users; looser admits impostors.
WHEN should you use it?
Device-local user verification (unlocking passkeys, payment approval) - not as a remote sole factor.

    FAR = sum(s >= threshold for s in impostor) / len(impostor)  # impostors ACCEPTED
    FRR = sum(s <  threshold for s in genuine)  / len(genuine)   # real users REJECTED

    far, frr = rates(t)
    print(f"threshold={t:.2f}  FAR={far:.1%}  FRR={frr:.1%}")

# The FAR==FRR point is the Equal Error Rate (EER) - how vendors compare sensors.
